definition: Non-representational moving laser patterns.
Continuous brightness control of each laser, usually 256 steps per color.
Repeated points at a line end or corner that give the scanners time to stop or turn.
A gas laser with strong blue and green lines, first seen working on February 14, 1964. The bright beam of 1970s rock tours.
A network transport for DMX lighting control data.
Beams deliberately swept through the crowd at levels meant to stay within the exposure limit. Excluded by the standard conditions of a US variance.
A laser show run from recorded control tracks, with nobody playing it. Lovelight (1977) is described as the first.
The blink or turn-away reflex to bright light. Exposure limits for visible beams assume it takes 0.25 seconds.
A 64 by 64 brightness map over a zone that dims or blocks output in chosen areas (Pangolin's term).
A show seen in mid-air: shapes scanned through haze as beams, fans, cones and tunnels.
A row of actuators that switch the beam to fixed positions, each aimed at a bounce mirror.
A surface or unit placed to catch a laser beam at the end of its path.
Switching the beam off while the scanners move between parts of an image.
The US Food and Drug Administration unit that inspected laser light shows in the late 1970s.
Running cues live to the music instead of playing back a time-coded show.
The FDA's Center for Devices and Radiological Health, which receives laser product reports and variance applications.
Above 5 mW up to 500 mW. Hazardous even for brief accidental direct exposure.
Up to 5 mW of visible output; the most a US show projector may emit without an FDA variance.
Above 500 mW. An eye and skin hazard from the direct or reflected beam, and often a fire hazard.
A scanner whose position detector feeds a servo amplifier that corrects the mirror.
Light waves lined up in time and space; the reason a laser beam spreads far less than ordinary light.
A gas laser used on large 1990s tours; Pink Floyd's 1994 US tour carried two 50 W systems.
FAA airspace within 10 NM of an airport up to 10,000 ft above ground, capped in Advisory Circular 70-1B at 5 microwatts/cm2.
Digital-to-analog converter: the hardware that turns software output into the voltages a projector takes.
The US legal term for a laser made, designed, intended or promoted for demonstration, entertainment, advertising display or artistic composition.
A mirror or filter that passes one color and reflects others; used to merge red, green and blue into one beam.
A ruled sheet that splits one beam into a fan of many. The Who's 1975 effect used a hand-held one.
A semiconductor chip that lases when current is applied to it, with no crystal in between.
How fast a beam widens as it travels. Doubling it halves the hazard distance.
Diode-pumped solid state: an 808 nm diode pumps a crystal lasing at 1064 nm, which a second crystal doubles to 532 nm green.
ILDA's award for technical achievement.
Visible strobing when a frame has so many points that it is redrawn too few times a second.
A thicker, billowing mist that shows swirls inside the beams.
One complete list of points for one image; frames played in sequence make animation.
Galvanometer scanner: a limited-rotation motor with a small mirror on its shaft. Two of them aim the beam.
Warping the output with sliders or a mesh so shapes land correctly on the target.
Dramatic performance rights - music used to tell a story, as in opera or musical theater. They are negotiated directly with the rights holder and are outside a blanket license.
A show in which the laser draws logos, text and animation on a surface.
A very fine, evenly spread mist that makes beams visible as smooth cones and sheets.
A low-power gas laser. Its red 632.8 nm line, found in 1962, gave the first continuous visible beam sold commercially.
A recording of the full wavefield of light that replays a true 3D image when lit by a laser.

ILDA Accredited Professional Lasershow Company: an industry credential requiring documented shows, client references, a staff member who has passed a Laser Safety Officer course and a signed safety affirmation.
ILDA Digital Network, a protocol for streaming laser graphics, effects and DMX data over a network.
ILDA Image Data Transfer Format, for exchanging laser show frames and files between systems.
The International Laser Display Association, the laser show trade body.
The laser display industry's annual prizes, with artistic categories such as Beams/Atmospherics, Graphics, Planetarium and Live Stage.
A standard frame, including a circle in a square, used to tune scanners and blanking at 12,000 or 30,000 points per second.
An FDA instruction that lets border staff detain listed firms' products without examining them; Import Alert 95-04 covers laser pointers and light show projectors.
An argon or krypton gas laser; the professional show source before solid state, water-cooled and about 0.05% efficient.
Power spread over an area, in mW/cm2. It falls with distance as a beam widens.
The 25-pin analog connection carrying X, Y, color, shutter and interlock signals to a projector.
Thousands of points per second, the scanner speed rating.
A gas laser that can give red, yellow, green and blue at once. Laserium split one krypton beam into four colors with prisms.
Laserists showing off their work to each other. First recorded on August 14, 1986.
Light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation: a source whose light is essentially one wavelength, with its waves in step, in a narrow beam.
The unit Guinness counts for its largest laser show record: each point where a beam leaves a device, with a beam split by diffraction counted once.
The usual name for a planetarium laser show set to Pink Floyd, most often Dark Side of the Moon or The Wall. Several companies have made their own.
FAA airspace closest to runways, where visible laser light is capped at 50 nW/cm2.
An instrument made of upright laser beams. Breaking a beam with the hand triggers a note.
Laser outlines fitted to the features of a building or 3D object.
A numbered FDA guidance letter to the laser industry, such as Notice 51 on projector sales or Notice 55 on variance renewal.
The named person responsible for laser safety at a facility or show. Required by name in several US states and in Germany.
A video projector in which blue laser diodes light a spinning phosphor wheel and an imaging chip forms the picture; no beam is scanned.
The person who performs or operates a laser show; in the analog era, the player of the console.
The laser show Ivan Dryer opened at Griffith Observatory in Los Angeles on November 19, 1973, played live to recorded music; it ran there until January 2002.
Laserium's analog performance console, with more than 150 controls for image size, motor speeds, brightness, shape and color, by one former laserist's count.
Laserium's first all-rock program, from 1977, and the start of the rock-album planetarium format.
Germany's laser safety officer, appointed in writing before Class 3R, 3B or 4 lasers are operated by an employer who lacks the required expertise personally.
The FAA's reply to a notice of an outdoor laser operation, stating an objection or no objection.
A scanning laser used to measure distance, as on some cars.
Haze or fog visibly swirling inside a flat sheet of scanned laser light.
A soft, gauze-like moving pattern made by sending a beam through rippled glass or plastic.
Metal plates at the aperture that cut off any output below or outside a set line, whatever the software sends.
The highest level of laser light a standard treats as acceptable for an eye or skin over a given time. For a visible beam and a quarter second it is about 2.5 mW/cm2.
The distance at which a direct beam has spread enough for its irradiance to fall to the MPE.
A notice to aircrews. The UK CAA normally issues one for a notified outdoor laser display.
Optically pumped semiconductor laser: diodes pump a thin gain chip in a small cavity, giving a clean, narrow beam and chosen colors such as 577 nm yellow.
Polychromatic acousto-optic modulator: a tellurium dioxide crystal driven by radio-frequency signals that set color and brightness on gas lasers.
A reflection illusion using a slanted transparent sheet; the method behind stage "holograms".
A body such as ASCAP, BMI, SESAC or Global Music Rights that licenses the public performance of songs to the business where the music is played.
The smallest thing laser software controls: an X position, a Y position, on or off, and usually a color.
One X-Y-color position sent to the projector. A frame is a list of them.
The condition lasing needs: more atoms in the excited state than in the ground state.
A named output area with its own size, position, geometric correction and safety settings.
An image built from closely spaced horizontal lines, as on a TV; too fast for scanner mirrors beyond low resolutions.
A generally analog console that lets the laserist change size, position, color and effects live.
The connector US law requires on Class IIIb and IV laser systems; an emergency stop plugs into it.
The first laser (1960): a pulsed red source at 694 nm. It flashes, so it was no use for drawing.
A person watching the airspace or beam paths who can terminate the beam immediately; ILDA's draft standard calls the role a laser spotter.
A safeguard that blanks the beam if the scanners stop moving it.
A system that cuts the beam if the scanning mirrors stop moving; listed by the UK HSE among standard controls for laser displays.
A feature that prevents exposure above the limits if the scanning mirrors slow or stop. Required on scanned laser products in the US by 21 CFR 1040.10(f)(9).
What a laser company charges per day of show, worked out from equipment write-off, overhead and margin.
A mechanical flag inside the projector that blocks the beam ahead of the scanners; the beam attenuator of the US rule.
The second person at a Laserium show, who followed a written script to time the house lights and the planetarium's star projector.
A passing photon makes an excited atom release a second photon matching it in wavelength, direction and phase.
A track on Laserium's four-track show tape that helped new laserists learn the timing.
A running clock signal, such as SMPTE or MIDI timecode, that keeps lasers, lights, video and audio on one timeline.
On/off-only laser control, giving seven colors and no fades.
A projector feature that lets the operator widen or narrow the beam during a show.
FDA permission to vary from a requirement of a performance standard - for shows, the 5 mW cap in 21 CFR 1040.11(c) - on stated safety conditions.
A requirement the FDA attaches to a variance approval, binding on the holder. The 3.0 m and 2.5 m audience separations are conditions.
A point with automatic sample placement: the software adds samples along long lines and at corners.
Images stored as points joined by lines and drawn as outlines.
A mixed argon/krypton ion laser that emits red, green and blue lines from one tube.
Drawing with one beam by steering it horizontally and vertically with two mirrors, the way an oscilloscope draws.
